transcription.tex: Separation of variables applies when the right-hand side is a product of one function of \(x\) and one of \(y\):\[\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x)g(y).\]For \(g(y)\ne0\), divide through:\[\frac1{g(y)}\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x).\]
Multiply by \(dx\) and integrate:\[\int\frac1{g(y)}\,dy=\int f(x)\,dx.\]Include an arbitrary integration constant. Check separately for constant solutions satisfying \(g(y)=0\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: Why is it called the general solution?
The arbitrary constant gives a family of solutions.
Find the general solution of \(dy/dx=-x/y\), where \(y\ne0\).
\[\int y\,dy=\int-x\,dx\]\[\tfrac12y^2=-\tfrac12x^2+C\]\[x^2+y^2=2C=r^2.\]The family of circles satisfies the equation wherever \(y\ne0\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: \[\frac{dy}{dx}=x(y+1)\]\[\int\frac1{y+1}\,dy=\int x\,dx\]\[\ln|y+1|=\tfrac12x^2+C\]\[|y+1|=e^{x^2/2+C}=e^{x^2/2}e^C\]\[y+1=Ae^{x^2/2}.\]Absorb the sign into real \(A\). Including \(A=0\) restores the equilibrium solution \(y=-1\).

\[\int\frac1y\,dy=\int-\frac1x\,dx\]\[\ln|y|=-\ln|x|+C\]\[\ln|x|+\ln|y|=C\]\[\ln|xy|=C\Rightarrow |xy|=e^C\]\[y=\frac A x,\quad A\in\mathbb R.\]This is a family of rectangular hyperbolas; \(A=0\) also gives a solution.

transcription.tex: We will solve \(y^{\prime}+Py=Q\), where \(P,Q\) are functions of \(x\). First practise reverse product rule.\par Find the general solution of \(x^3y^{\prime}+3x^2y=\sin x\). The variables do not separate. What do you notice about the left-hand side?
The coefficient of \(y^{\prime}\) becomes the factor multiplying \(y\) inside the derivative.

transcription.tex: For \(y^{\prime}+Py=Q\), suppose \(f(x)\) is an integrating factor. Multiply through:\[fy^{\prime}+fPy=fQ.\]To use reverse product rule, the left side must equal \(fy^{\prime}+f^{\prime}y\).
Choose \(f>0\), divide and integrate:\[\int\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\int P\,dx\]\[\ln f(x)=\int P\,dx.\]
\[f(x)=e^{\int P\,dx}.\]A non-zero constant multiplier does not affect the method.

slides.title: When the Derivative Has a Coefficient

transcription.tex: Solve \(\cos x\,y^{\prime}+2y\sin x=\cos^4x\). What should we do first?
1. Divide by \(\cos x\), on intervals where it is non-zero:\[y^{\prime}+2y\tan x=\cos^3x.\]
3. Multiply through:\[\sec^2x\,y^{\prime}+2y\sec^2x\tan x=\cos x\]\[\frac d{dx}(y\sec^2x)=\cos x.\]You can go straight to this derivative, but remember to multiply the right side by the factor too.

transcription.tex: Edexcel FP2 (Old), June 2011 Q3\par Find the general solution of\[xy^{\prime}+5y=\frac{\ln x}{x},\quad x>0.\]

Integrate by parts:\[\int x^3\ln x\,dx=\frac{x^4\ln x}4-\int\frac{x^3}4\,dx\]\[=\frac{x^4\ln x}4-\frac{x^4}{16}+C.\]\[x^5y=\frac{x^4\ln x}4-\frac{x^4}{16}+C\]\[y=\frac{\ln x}{4x}-\frac1{16x}+\frac C{x^5}.\]

transcription.tex: Second-order differential equations involve a second derivative.\par Car shock absorbers provide an example. Damping opposes velocity; the restoring spring force opposes displacement from equilibrium. Their magnitudes are proportional to velocity and extension respectively.
Take downward displacement \(x\) as positive, measured from equilibrium. Newton’s second law gives:
For \(x>0\) and \(\dot x>0\), both forces and the resulting acceleration are upward. Positive coordinate direction does not specify actual acceleration.

transcription.tex: For \(ay^{\prime}+by=0\), the solution is \(y=Ae^{-bx/a}\). Try a similar form for\[ay^{\prime\prime}+by^{\prime}+cy=0,\quad a\ne0.\]Let \(y=Ae^{mx}\).
For a non-zero trial solution, \(A\ne0\), so\[am^2+bm+c=0.\]This is the auxiliary equation: its roots determine the solutions of the differential equation.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: If \(m\) is a root of \(am^2+bm+c=0\), then \(Ae^{mx}\) solves \(ay^{\prime\prime}+by^{\prime}+cy=0\).\par For distinct real roots \(\alpha,\beta\):\[y=Ae^{\alpha x}+Be^{\beta x}.\]Here \(A,B\) are arbitrary constants.\par A zero right-hand side makes the equation homogeneous.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: For two equal roots \(\alpha\), where \(b^2-4ac=0\):\[y=(A+Bx)e^{\alpha x}.\]Show that \((A+Bx)e^{3x}\) satisfies\[y^{\prime\prime}-6y^{\prime}+9y=0.\]The auxiliary equation is \((m-3)^2=0\).

Why not \(Ae^{\alpha x}+Be^{\alpha x}\)? It combines to just one arbitrary constant. The extra \(x\) gives an independent solution, analogous to the distinct terms \(A/x+B/x^2\) used for repeated partial-fraction factors.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: Complex roots work similarly to distinct real roots. Solve \(y^{\prime\prime}+16y=0\).
Using Euler’s formula:\[y=A(\cos4x+i\sin4x)\]\[+B(\cos4x-i\sin4x)\]\[=P\cos4x+Q\sin4x,\]\[P=A+B,\quad Q=i(A-B).\]For real solutions, take \(P,Q\) real.

transcription.tex: Use Euler’s formula and factor out \(e^{3x}\):\[y=e^{3x}(P\cos5x+Q\sin5x).\]
For roots \(p\pm iq\):\[y=e^{px}(A\cos qx+B\sin qx),\]with real arbitrary constants \(A,B\).

transcription.tex: What if the right-hand side is a function of \(x\)?\[ay^{\prime\prime}+by^{\prime}+cy=f(x).\]This is non-homogeneous when \(f\) is not identically zero.\par First solve the homogeneous equation:\[ay^{\prime\prime}+by^{\prime}+cy=0.\]Its general solution is the complementary function (CF).

Next find one solution of\[ay^{\prime\prime}+by^{\prime}+cy=f(x)\]by choosing an appropriate trial function and comparing coefficients. This is the particular integral (PI).\[y=\mathrm{CF}+\mathrm{PI}.\]The differential operator gives zero for the CF and \(f(x)\) for the PI; adding gives \(f(x)\).

transcription.tex: A trial PI cannot already belong to the CF. This is like needing independent solutions for repeated auxiliary roots.\par Solve \(y^{\prime\prime}-5y^{\prime}+6y=e^{2x}\).\par The CF is \(Ae^{2x}+Be^{3x}\). What goes wrong if we try \(y=\lambda e^{2x}\)?
Then\[y=(A+\lambda)e^{2x}+Be^{3x}.\]This is still just the CF: substitution gives \(0=e^{2x}\), impossible.

transcription.tex: June 2012 Q4\par Find the general solution of\[\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}+5\frac{dx}{dt}+6x=2\cos t-\sin t.\]Here \(x\) is the dependent variable and \(t\) the independent variable.

\[m^2+5m+6=0\Rightarrow m=-2,-3\]\[\mathrm{CF}=Ae^{-2t}+Be^{-3t}.\]Try \(x=P\cos t+Q\sin t\):\[\dot x=-P\sin t+Q\cos t,\quad\ddot x=-P\cos t-Q\sin t.\]\[(-P\cos t-Q\sin t)+5(-P\sin t+Q\cos t)\]\[+6(P\cos t+Q\sin t)=2\cos t-\sin t.\]\[-P+5Q+6P=2,\quad-Q-5P+6Q=-1\]\[5P+5Q=2,\quad-5P+5Q=-1\]\[P=\tfrac3{10},\quad Q=\tfrac1{10}.\]\[x=Ae^{-2t}+Be^{-3t}+\tfrac3{10}\cos t+\tfrac1{10}\sin t.\]
